The delayed obliteration of the arterial lumen may occur by one of several mechanisms, and it's essential to consider the various factors that contribute to this process. The roughened or torn arterial intima attracts platelets, fibrin, and red cells, resulting in a traumatic thrombosis, which can lead to a range of complications. Moreover, the flow of blood may elevate the torn distal end of the intima, creating a subintimal dissection that can further compromise the integrity of the artery. Additionally, even though the inner and outer coats of the artery remain intact, an intramural hematoma may form that obliterates the lumen of the artery, leading to a complete blockage of blood flow. Furthermore, the presence of atherosclerotic plaques or other vascular lesions can exacerbate the obliteration of the lumen, making it more challenging to treat. Notably, the severity of the obliteration can vary depending on the underlying cause, and prompt medical attention is necessary to prevent long-term damage to the artery.
